nameStory: Wood Fingerwort gets its name from its tiny, finger-like leafy shoots that branch and divide like miniature hands reaching through the forest floor. The 'wort' part is an old English word meaning 'plant,' historically used for small, humble plants that early botanists thought looked useful but weren't quite sure what to do with.
description: Wood Fingerwort is a tiny leafy liverwort that forms small, delicate patches on rotting logs and moist soil in shaded forests. This diminutive plant rarely grows taller than your thumbnail, creating intricate branching patterns that look like microscopic green coral. Its leaves are so small you'll need to look closely to see the detailed structure, but once you spot it, you'll notice how it creates lovely textured carpets in its favorite spots.

idTips.label: Finger-like branching
idTips.description: Shoots branch repeatedly in a distinctive pattern that resembles tiny green fingers or antlers, with each branch getting progressively smaller toward the tips

idTips.label: Microscopic scale
idTips.description: Extremely small - individual plants are usually less than 1cm tall, requiring you to get down close and look carefully to see the intricate details

idTips.label: Overlapping leaves
idTips.description: Tiny leaves overlap like shingles on a roof, giving shoots a slightly flattened, scaly texture when viewed with a hand lens

idTips.label: Substrate preference
idTips.description: Almost always found growing directly on very soft, punk-like decaying wood that feels spongy and crumbles easily when touched

idTips.label: Colony formation
idTips.description: Forms small but distinct patches or colonies, creating textured green areas that stand out against the brown decay beneath

habitat: Wood Fingerwort thrives in deep, shaded hardwood forests on very decayed logs, stumps, and occasionally rich humus soil. Look for it in mature forest areas with plenty of fallen timber, especially where logs have been decomposing for several years and feel soft and spongy. It prefers consistently moist but not waterlogged conditions in areas that rarely see direct sunlight.

seasonality.spring: Most visible as winter moisture gives way to spring dampness, when colonies appear fresh and bright green on newly-softened winter deadfall.
seasonality.summer: May be harder to spot as forest floor dries out, but persists in consistently moist microsites around large decaying logs and in deep shade.
seasonality.fall: Often more noticeable again as autumn rains return and new patches establish on recently fallen branches and logs from summer storms.
seasonality.winter: Remains green under snow cover and can be found year-round, though growth slows significantly in cold weather.

funFact: Despite being smaller than most postage stamps, Wood Fingerwort is actually helping to digest entire fallen trees - it's part of a microscopic ecosystem that can completely break down a massive oak trunk over decades, essentially eating the forest from the inside out one tiny bite at a time.
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with other tiny leafy liverworts on rotting wood, but Wood Fingerwort's distinctive finger-like branching pattern sets it apart from the more irregularly branched or simply forked growth of its relatives. Memory trick: 'Fingers in the forest' - look for that hand-like branching pattern.
contextualKnowledge: Like other liverworts, this is actually more closely related to mosses than to flowering plants, representing one of the earliest forms of land plants that evolved hundreds of millions of years ago. The term 'liverwort' comes from medieval beliefs that plants shaped like body parts could cure ailments of those organs, though these tiny plants bear little resemblance to anything anatomical.
compareHints: Wood Fingerwort is the only Kurzia species regularly found in New England, but it can be distinguished from similar tiny leafy liverworts in the same family by its very regular, repeatedly forked branching pattern. Other small liverworts on wood tend to have more irregular growth patterns or differently shaped leaves that don't create the same finger-like appearance.
